"authors": "Joy S Zeng, Vineet Padia, Joseph H Maalouf, Aditya M Limaye, Alexander H Liu, Michael A Yusov, Ian W Hunter, Karthish Manthiram",

"executive_summary": "Electrocatalytic mechanism studies traditionally lean on linearized rate data, which underpins Tafel and reactant order dependence analyses. These linearization strategies assume that dependences on different experimental handles can be factored separately and linearized on log-log or semi-log graphs. However, for complex phenomena such as surface coverage effects or mixed control, these common linearization strategies will yield incomplete or uninterpretable results. Cohesive kinetic analysis, which is often used in thermocatalysis and involves quantitative model fitting for data collected over a wide range of reaction conditions, requires more data but also provides a more robust strategy for interrogating reaction mechanisms. In this work, the authors report a robotic system that improves the experimental workflow for collecting electrochemical rate data by automating sequential testing of up to ten electrochemical cells that can each have a different electrode, electrolyte, gas-phase reactant composition, and applied voltage. They use this system to investigate the mechanism of carbon dioxide electroreduction to carbon monoxide at several immobilized metal tetrapyrroles. Specifically, at cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc), cobalt tetraphenylporphyrin (CoTPP), and iron phthalocyanine (FePc), they see signatures of complex reaction mechanisms, where observed bicarbonate and CO2 order dependences change with applied potential. They illustrate how phenomena such as electrolyte poisoning and potential-dependent degrees of rate control can explain the observed kinetic behaviors. Their mechanistic analysis suggests that CoPc and CoTPP share a similar reaction mechanism, akin to one that has been previously proposed, whereas the mechanism for FePc likely involves a species later in the catalytic cycle as the most abundant reactive intermediate. Their study illustrates that complex reaction mechanisms which are not amenable to common Tafel and order dependence analyses may be quite prevalent across this class of immobilized metal tetrapyrrole electrocatalysts.",

summary.title: Non-idealities in CO2 electroreduction mechanisms revealed by automation-assisted kinetic analysis
summary.authors: Joy S Zeng, Vineet Padia, Joseph H Maalouf, Aditya M Limaye, Alexander H Liu, Michael A Yusov, Ian W Hunter, Karthish Manthiram
summary.executive_summary: Electrocatalytic mechanism studies traditionally lean on linearized rate data, which underpins Tafel and reactant order dependence analyses. These linearization strategies assume that dependences on different experimental handles can be factored separately and linearized on log-log or semi-log graphs. However, for complex phenomena such as surface coverage effects or mixed control, these common linearization strategies will yield incomplete or uninterpretable results. Cohesive kinetic analysis, which is often used in thermocatalysis and involves quantitative model fitting for data collected over a wide range of reaction conditions, requires more data but also provides a more robust strategy for interrogating reaction mechanisms. In this work, the authors report a robotic system that improves the experimental workflow for collecting electrochemical rate data by automating sequential testing of up to ten electrochemical cells that can each have a different electrode, electrolyte, gas-phase reactant composition, and applied voltage. They use this system to investigate the mechanism of carbon dioxide electroreduction to carbon monoxide at several immobilized metal tetrapyrroles. Specifically, at cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc), cobalt tetraphenylporphyrin (CoTPP), and iron phthalocyanine (FePc), they see signatures of complex reaction mechanisms, where observed bicarbonate and CO2 order dependences change with applied potential. They illustrate how phenomena such as electrolyte poisoning and potential-dependent degrees of rate control can explain the observed kinetic behaviors. Their mechanistic analysis suggests that CoPc and CoTPP share a similar reaction mechanism, akin to one that has been previously proposed, whereas the mechanism for FePc likely involves a species later in the catalytic cycle as the most abundant reactive intermediate. Their study illustrates that complex reaction mechanisms which are not amenable to common Tafel and order dependence analyses may be quite prevalent across this class of immobilized metal tetrapyrrole electrocatalysts.

Their study illustrates that complex reaction mechanisms which are not amenable to common Tafel and order dependence analyses may be quite prevalent across this class of immobilized metal tetrapyrrole electrocatalysts.

Research Context
Electrocatalysis has traditionally relied on linearized rate data for mechanistic interpretation. Tafel and reactant order dependence analyses assume factorable, linearizable dependences. Coverage effects, mixed rate control, and side reactions complicate linearization. Cohesive kinetic analysis is common in thermocatalysis but rare in electrocatalysis. A meta-analysis showed Tafel slopes lack interpretable values, hinting at hidden complexity. Prior cohesive analysis revealed competitive electrolyte adsorption and mixed control for CO2RR to CO on CoPc.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Do non-ideal kinetic signatures (non-linear, potential-dependent orders) appear across immobilized metal tetrapyrroles? Can automation enable cohesive kinetic analysis of individual cells with online product quantification? Do bicarbonate and CO2 orders change with applied potential across CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc? Can electrolyte poisoning and potential-dependent mixed control explain these trends? Do CoPc and CoTPP share a mechanism, while FePc involves a later-cycle intermediate?

Methodological Details
Catalysts were immobilized on calcined Toray060 carbon paper working electrodes. CoPc was loaded at 5.98 x 10^-11 mol/cm^2. CoTPP and FePc were loaded at 5.11 x 10^-10 and 8.04 x 10^-10 mol/cm^2. Carbon black was added to less active catalysts to increase loading and avoid aggregation. Catalysts were dissolved in DMF or carbon black-containing DMF. Stock solutions of 0.5 mol/L Na2CO3 and 1 mol/L NaClO4 were prepared. Stock solutions were bubbled overnight with CO2 before use. Electrolytes had overall 1 mol/L ionic strength with varied bicarbonate concentrations. The robot tested up to ten cells sequentially in a single effort. The working electrode was a 10 mm diameter carbon paper disk. The reference electrode was a leak-free Ag/AgCl calibrated against SCE daily. The counter electrode was a 0.25 mm diameter platinum wire. Online product quantification used a gas chromatograph for CO and H2. All data were uploaded to an SQL database and processed with a python script. Data were output as average current, partial CO current, and partial H2 current.

Procedures And Architectures
The robot houses a single cell body with a line of ten cell pan pairs. The cell body moves horizontally and vertically to sequence experiments. Electrolyte flows through the electrolyte in port, then gas flows through the gas in tubing. A gas chromatograph connected to the gas out port detects CO and H2. The cell body rinses at a wash station with milliQ water after ten runs. The cell assembly is analogous to a three-electrode, undivided compartment cell. The lack of a membrane allowed more facile liquid and gas management. Without a membrane, oxygen from the counter electrode can cause parasitic ORR. Incomplete FE closure averaged about 60% attributable to CO and H2. A Pt counter electrode was chosen to preclude adventitious anode oxidation products. High FEs toward HER were typically around 30 to 60%. CO2 was bubbled into the electrolyte rather than fed directly to the electrode. Currents were below the theoretical mass transport limited current density. CoPc data were compared against previously reported manually collected results. Newly measured CO rates were up to ten times lower than previously reported. New CO FEs were typically under 30%. Previously reported kinetic trends in CO production were preserved.

Key Results
CoPc and CoTPP show most negative bicarbonate dependence at less reductive potentials. CoTPP and CoPc bicarbonate dependence becomes positive at more reductive potentials. FePc shows greater bicarbonate inhibition at more reductive potentials. CoPc and CoTPP bicarbonate orders change sign with potential, indicating mixed control. FePc bicarbonate inhibition is amplified at more reductive potentials, unlike local adsorption. FePc trends can be explained by a MARI prior to the unoccupied site. CoPc shows a simple first order CO2 dependence within error at both potentials. CoTPP CO2 order is slightly below one and decreases at more reductive potentials. CoTPP CO2 attenuation is characteristic of surface saturation effects. FePc CO2 order is most unusual, attenuated at less reductive potentials. FePc CO2 order curves for two potentials intersect, indicating voltage inhibition at low CO2. FePc mixed control invokes an on-cycle poisoning species with net negative voltage effect. Non-linear, potential-dependent orders were observed across all three catalysts. CoPc showed curvature and potential-dependent bicarbonate order changes.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Bicarbonate poisoning via adsorption onto an unoccupied site explains CoPc and CoTPP. Positive electrosorption valency means less bicarbonate adsorption at more reductive potentials. Potential-dependent mixed control explains the sign change in bicarbonate order. FePc requires a MARI prior to the unoccupied site to explain amplified inhibition. On-cycle poisoning species can attenuate or amplify bicarbonate dependence. Surface saturation effects attenuate apparent CO2 order for CoTPP. Mixed control with on-cycle poisoning explains intersecting FePc CO2 curves. CoPc and CoTPP share a mechanism akin to a previously proposed one. FePc likely involves a species later in the catalytic cycle as the MARI. Complex mechanisms not amenable to Tafel analysis may be prevalent across tetrapyrroles.

Contradictions And Limitations
Newly measured CO rates were up to ten times lower than previously reported. New CO FEs were typically under 30%, indicating incomplete FE closure. Incomplete FE closure averaged about 60% attributable to CO and H2. High HER FEs of 30 to 60% may confound partial CO current interpretation. Undivided cell allows crosstalk and parasitic ORR from the counter electrode. Currents were below mass transport limit, yet flow configuration may still influence kinetics. Proposed mechanisms only qualitatively capture trends, not via statistical goodness-of-fit. Proposed mechanisms do not quantitatively fit all experimental data. No specific reaction mechanism is proposed; only conceptual discussion is provided. The study is a single-compartment cell, unlike conventional divided cells.

Claims
Automation enables cohesive kinetic analysis of individual electrochemical cells with online product quantification. The robot automates sequential testing of up to ten cells. Online product quantification uses a gas chromatograph for CO and H2. Data were uploaded to an SQL database and processed with a python script. The workflow enables faster and more facile rate data collection. Automation strategies are often tailored to high-throughput screening. Small working volumes hinder product quantification for non-100% FE reactions. Automation standardizes and accelerates cohesive kinetic analysis. Future software could enumerate mechanisms and suggest informative conditions.
CoPc and CoTPP share a mechanism with potential-dependent mixed control and bicarbonate poisoning. CoPc and CoTPP bicarbonate dependence becomes positive at more reductive potentials. CoPc and CoTPP invoke bicarbonate poisoning and potential-dependent mixed control. Such a model has previously been reported to quantitatively describe CoPc kinetics. FePc shows opposite bicarbonate inhibition trends, indicating a different mechanism. CoPc and CoTPP kinetics can be reconciled by a shared mechanism. Potential-dependent mixed control explains sign changes in bicarbonate order.
FePc involves a MARI prior to the unoccupied site, explaining amplified bicarbonate inhibition. FePc shows greater bicarbonate inhibition at more reductive potentials. FePc trends require a MARI prior to the unoccupied site. Conversion of the MARI to the unoccupied site has stronger voltage dependence. FePc trends contradict local bicarbonate adsorption equilibrium expectations. FePc mechanism differs from CoPc and CoTPP. MARI position affects potential-dependent inhibition trends.
Complex, non-ideal mechanisms are prevalent across immobilized metal tetrapyrroles. Non-linear, potential-dependent orders were observed across all three catalysts. Such signatures have only been reported in one previous work at CoPc. Trends are unexplainable with mechanisms typically invoked for CO2RR at tetrapyrroles. CoPc showed a simple first order CO2 dependence within error. Tafel analysis may miss prevalent mechanistic complexity. Ostensibly opposing observations may be reconciled by operating conditions.

Data And Code Availability
All experimental data reported in this work is available as xlsx. Reagent information and detailed protocols are in the supporting information. The work is licensed under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Supplemental discussion 5 includes derivations and fittings of the models.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
CoPc data were validated against previously reported manually collected results. Previously reported kinetic trends in CO production were preserved. New data was well-correlated with previous work. Curvature and potential-dependent bicarbonate orders were evident in validation data. Aggregated rates and selectivities were provided for all three catalysts.

Ethical Considerations
The work is licensed under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Content was not peer-reviewed by ChemRxiv. The work was submitted to ChemRxiv.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the overall robot design with a single cell body. Figure 1B shows the cell assembly analogous to a three-electrode cell. Figure 1B shows electrolyte and gas flow through the cell body. Figure 2A-C show voltage-dependent bicarbonate inhibition across catalysts. Figure 2D-E show off-cycle poisoning mechanisms for CoPc and CoTPP. Figure 2F-G show on-cycle poisoning mechanisms for CoPc and FePc. Figure 3A-C show CO2 order dependences for all three catalysts. Figure 3D shows surface saturation effects for CoTPP. Figure 3E shows mixed control with on-cycle poisoning for FePc.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a robotic platform enabling cohesive kinetic analysis of individual cells with online product quantification. 2. The strongest evidence is the observation of non-linear, potential-dependent bicarbonate and CO2 orders across CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc. 3. The future path involves incorporating a membrane, alternative flow configurations, and software to enumerate mechanisms.
